turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, let's get your numbers done before you go in. Arm out for me, please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, the cuff. I always think it's going to pop. We were sat out there and that telly was so loud I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Blood pressure is one hundred and thirty eight over eighty two. Pulse seventy eight. Temperature thirty six point eight, and your sats are ninety seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety seven, I'll take that. I'm seventy two, you know, seventy three next birthday.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She tells everyone her age. It's her party trick.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): You're all set. The doctor will call you in a tick.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Have a seat, both of you. What brings you in today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this burning, doctor, on the one side. Left side of my chest, like a hot coal under the skin. And a few little blisters have come up.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Burning on the left side of the chest, plus some blisters. When did that start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The burning's been two days. The blisters, um, I spotted them yesterday morning.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, she rang me yesterday in a flap. It really is only two days, not longer.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I've overdone it, I reckon, lugging those pots about in the garden. Then I thought, ooh, my back's gone. No, actually, the back's fine, it's just this chest.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the gardening was your first idea, but the pain is in the chest, not the back. Have you felt feverish?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I feel like a wet rag, honestly. Washed out. But no, no fever, I checked with the thermometer and it was normal.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tired, then, but no fever. Is the skin itchy, or is it only the burning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Itchy as well. I want to scratch and then I stop myself. There's only a handful, five or six blisters, all on the left, none round the other side.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or pain when you breathe in, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's easy. No cough.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And otherwise, any problem with your tummy or your waterworks?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, tummy's fine, waterworks fine. Oh, but I've had a frog in my throat all week, all croaky. Probably the dust off those pots.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been croaky, yes. The chest is what we came about, though.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Croaky for a week, and the chest for two days. May I have a look at the rash?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. Mind, my feet feel dead from that waiting room chair. That's just the chair, not my feet playing up.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the chair out of it. On the left chest there's a band of red skin with a few small clear blisters, and it stops at the midline. It's tender where I press.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yes, that's the bit.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Did you have chickenpox as a child?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Lord, yes. I was about seven, covered in spots. Mum painted me in calamine and shut the curtains, and I haven't had it since.

[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): While we're on tablets, doctor, don't put her on biotin. Those gummies are my sister Claire's, for her hair. Mum nearly took one this morning, thinking it was the blood pressure pill.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take it, I only looked at the jar. Claire was round yesterday, six months pregnant, and she gave me a great hug, the daft thing.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): All right. Claire's biotin is Claire's, and you didn't swallow any. Your sister is pregnant and she saw you yesterday. What do you take for your blood pressure?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine. Err, five milligrams, I think. I've had high blood pressure for years. Little white tablet in the mornings.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's meant to take it every morning, but if she's out in the garden she skips it. I wouldn't swear she's had it every day this week.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine five milligrams each morning, though a dose gets missed now and then. Anything for the pain?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two five hundred milligram tablets, four times a day, since yesterday. It helps a bit, not loads.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol one gram, four times a day. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I come up in a rash, big red blotches. I stay right away from it.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Penicillin with a rash, thank you. Any pain in the eye, or spots creeping up near it?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing near the eye. Eyes are fine.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. My first thought was to swab those blisters and hold off the antivirals till the result came back, just some calamine on the skin meanwhile.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): But Claire's pregnant, and this only started two days ago. She was all over Mum yesterday.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want to pass anything on. Claire's never had chickenpox, she told me so.

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): That changes it. Forget the swab, and forget waiting on a result. This is shingles, I think, herpes zoster on the left chest, with the one-sided burning, the blisters, and chickenpox as a child.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles. My neighbour had that and she was miserable for weeks, wouldn't even chat over the fence. Are you giving me something today, then?
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, today. I'll start you on valaciclovir, one gram by mouth, three times a day, for seven days. You're still inside the seventy two hours, so it's worth it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Vala-sicky-veer, is that how you say it? Will the chemist actually have it in?
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Valaciclovir, yes, and they should. Carry on with the paracetamol, up to four times a day, and try not to scratch.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): The other bit is Claire. Keep the rash covered, don't share towels, and no close contact with her until those blisters have crusted. If she's never had chickenpox she could catch it from you, and that's risky in pregnancy.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll text her to stay away. What about seeing Mum again?

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a week, to check the rash is crusting and the tablets suit you. If it spreads toward the eye, or you get feverish or muddled, ring the surgery the same day, don't wait for that appointment.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A week I can do. The garden can mind itself. I'll try not to start on the pots again.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll sort a blister pack so the amlodipine actually gets swallowed, and I'll take Claire's biotin back to mine.

[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Two days of burning on the left chest, a few blisters in a band, no fever, no breathlessness, chickenpox as a child, a penicillin rash, amlodipine and paracetamol. Shingles, valaciclovir from today, stay clear of your pregnant sister till it crusts, and back in a week.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): You've got the lot. Thanks, doctor. Come on, love, before I get going about those pots again.

spec.situation: Older person with burning pain on one side of the chest and a few blisters for two days; remembers chickenpox as a child; doctor prescribes antiviral today and gives infection advice about contact with a pregnant relative.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Amlodipine 5 mg each morning for blood pressure stated, but patient was unsure of the dose.
bad.text: amlodipine (dose=5 mg, frequency=every morning, indication=high blood pressure, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Doctor says ring if rash spreads toward eye or if feverish or muddled; 'confused' wording not explicit.
bad.text: Ring the surgery the same day if the rash spreads toward the eye or if feverish or confused (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Rash details not recorded: patient said there were only about five or six blisters, all on the left and not going around to the other side.
Exam detail not recorded: the rash stopped at the midline.
Past history not recorded: patient had chickenpox as a child (about age 7).
Penicillin allergy reaction was described as a rash with big red blotches, not just unspecified rash.

There was an initial management plan discussed and then changed: doctor first proposed swabbing the blisters and holding antivirals pending the result, with calamine in the meantime, but reversed this after learning about the pregnant sister's exposure.
Calamine was mentioned as symptomatic treatment in the initial plan and is not recorded.
Reason for starting antivirals now not recorded: doctor said the patient was still within 72 hours so treatment was worth it.
